newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FOCUS-Ashanti considers Ivorian gold, energy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ashanti considers Ivorian gold, energy.

text.p: Ghana's Ashanti Goldfields Ltd said on Thursday it will take up an invitation from Ivory Coast to invest in gold exploration in the neighbouring country.
It would also consider importing gas or electricity from Ivory Coast to overcome power shortages in Ghana, a spokesman told Reuters on Thursday.

The plans were revealed after Ashanti managing director Sam Jonah, leading a Ghanaian delegation, ended talks this week with Ivorian President Henri Konan Bedie and mines and energy minister Lamine Fadika in Abidjan.
"As soon as possible our geologists will be going there to look," Ashanti spokesman James Anaman said after the talks.
"There has been an ever-increasing demand for power in Ghana and that is affecting the regular supply of power (to Ashanti)."

Ivory Coast wants to broaden its farm-based economy by expanding mining, energy, and food processing. It opened a Mines Commission in April similar to Ghana's after prospectors' complaints about red tape during mining permit applications.
Around 65 mining exploration permits have been issued to a total of over 25 firms, many of which have arrived since a new mining code in 1995, mining officials told Reuters.
Ivorian annual gold output remains less than a tenth of Ghana's at around three tonnes from two mines in production. A third mine is planned to open in 1997.

"We have promised to look at their resources and commit the necessary funds for exploration," Anaman told Reuters by telephone from Accra. "We have been invited to look wherever we like after consultation with our geologists."
A decision on exploration hangs on geologists' advice.
Ashanti, West Africa's largest gold miner, already has three mines in Ghana and one in Zimbabwe and plans to bring on line two new West African gold mines in 1998.
"We are already operating in 15 African countries. Why should it be any different in Ivory Coast?" the Ivorian government daily paper Fraternite Matin quoted Jonah as saying.
Ashanti also has 35 exploration projects in 12 African countries at various levels of development with a mine project at Geita in Tanzania the most advanced, Anaman said.

Two mines, in Guinea and Ghana, are planned to open in 1998, said Anaman, adding that Niger, Burkina Faso, Guinea and then Mali were the most promising exploration areas in Ashanti's home base of West Africa.

Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, shares an eastern border with Ghana and overlies similar gold-bearing Birimian greenstone geology. Its growing oil and gas fields are within a few hundred kilometres of Ashanti in southern Ghana.
Jonah also visited Ivory Coast's national petroleum company Petroci and U.S.-based United Meridian Corporation (UMIC-CI).
A long-term regional plan for energy integration could mean a gas pipeline will extend from Mauritania to eastern Nigeria's abundant gas fields where large volumes are flared.
"We have just discussed opportunities available to Ashanti," Anaman said, adding that any decision on gas or energy imports would be price-dependent.
UMIC earlier this year submitted a bid for supplying gas to a 200 MW power plant being built in Takoradi, western Ghana.
"We can have (Ivorian) gas in Takoradi in 18 months," a UMIC official said at an energy conference in Ghana in April.

"There could be a lot of natural gas in Shell's CI 105 block in (eastern) Ivory Coast, while Shell also has a lot of gas in Nigeria. Together we can start building the West Africa Pipeline from both ends and meet in Ghana, " said another.
Ivory Coast's Compagnie d'Electricite Ivoirienne (CIE) predicts Ivory Coast will export energy to its neighbours after completion of a new power plant planned for Abidjan.

"Ivory Coast has about 1,200 megawatts (MW) installed but there are no large industrial users," a West Africa-based manager for Swedish power group Asea Brown Boveri (ABB) told Reuters. "One of the top 10 power consumers is a hotel."
ABB was one winning bidder recently named to build the Abidjan plant.
